claims.text: High-strain-rate rolling followed by short-duration sub-critical annealing will simultaneously enhance strength and plasticity in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The starting refractory high-entropy alloy has relatively coarse grains.
The starting alloy has an unoptimized dislocation structure.
High-strain-rate rolling introduces severe plastic deformation.
High-strain-rate rolling refines the grain structure.
Annealing below the full-recrystallization threshold permits limited recovery without full recrystallization.
Sub-critical annealing can induce precipitation in refractory high-entropy alloys such as Mo-Nb-Ta-W systems.
The combined treatment produces a refined microstructure with reduced grain size.
Rolling increases dislocation density.
Short sub-critical annealing forms nanoscale precipitates or fine thermally induced substructures.
Grain refinement caused by severe plastic deformation increases yield strength.
Rolling-induced dislocations increase yield strength.
Annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Avoiding full recrystallization prevents excessive softening.
Partial recovery and precipitation after rolling can maintain or enhance uniform ductility while improving strength.
The combined treatment will produce a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to an untreated or conventionally processed baseline.
The combined treatment will maintain or improve uniform elongation relative to an untreated or conventionally processed baseline.
Both rolling and controlled sub-critical annealing are required to obtain the proposed enhancement.
Insufficient deformation may fail to produce the proposed strength-plasticity balance.
An annealing temperature that is too high may fail to produce the proposed strength-plasticity balance.
